title: Estimating wind-turbine-caused bird and bat fatality when zero carcasses are observed
abstract: Many wind-power facilities in the United States have established effective monitoring programs to determine turbine-caused fatality rates of birds and bats, but estimating the number of fatalities of rare species poses special difficulties. The loss of even small numbers of individuals may adversely affect fragile populations, but typically, few (if any) carcasses are observed during monitoring. If monitoring design results in only a small proportion of carcasses detected, then finding zero carcasses may give little assurance that the number of actual fatalities is small. Fatality monitoring at wind-power facilities commonly involves conducting experiments to estimate the probability (g) an individual will be observed, accounting for the possibilities that it falls in an unsearched area, is scavenged prior to detection, or remains undetected even when present. When g < 1, the total carcass count (X) underestimates the total number of fatalities (M). Total counts can be 0 when M is small or when M is large and g ≪1. Distinguishing these two cases is critical when estimating fatality of a rare species. Observing no individuals during searches may erroneously be interpreted as evidence of absence. We present an approach that uses Bayes' theorem to construct a posterior distribution for M, i.e., P(M | X, ĝ), reflecting the observed carcass count and previously estimated g. From this distribution, we calculate two values important to conservation: the probability that M is below a predetermined limit and the upper bound (M*) of the 100(1 − α)% credible interval for M. We investigate the dependence of M* on α, g, and the prior distribution of M, asking what value of g is required to attain a desired M* for a given α. We found that when g < −0.15, M* was clearly influenced by the mean and variance of ĝ and the choice of prior distribution for M, but the influence of these factors is minimal when g > −0.45. Further, we develop extensions for temporal replication that can inform prior distributions of M and methods for combining information across several areas or time periods. We apply the method to data collected at a wind-power facility where scheduled searches yielded X = 0 raptor carcasses.

## 49 **INTRODUCTION**

50 Wind turbines have long been known to pose a threat to passing bats and birds (Hall &

- 51 Richards 1972; Rogers et al. 1977). They have been implicated in lethal takes of several species

- 52 protected under the US Endangered Species Act (ESA), including the Hawaiian petrel

- 53 _(Pterodroma sandwichensis_ ), Hawaiian goose ( _Branta sandvicensis_ ), Hawaiian hoary bat

- 54 ( _Lasiurus cinereus semotus_ ) (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2011b) and the Indiana bat ( _Myotis_

- 55 _sodalis_ ) (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2014b). There is also concern about endangered species

- 56 that live near wind power facilities but have not been reported as casualties, including the

- 57 California condor ( _Gymnogyps californianus_ ) (Barringer 2013; U.S. Bureau of Land

- 58 Management 2013), whooping crane ( _Grus americana_ ) (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2011a),

- 59 and several lesser-known species, such as the Virginia big-eared bat ( _Corynorhinus townsendii_

- 60 _virginianus_ ), gray bat ( _Myotis grisescens_ ), piping plover ( _Charadrius melodus_ ), interior least tern

- 61 ( _Sterna antillarum athalassos_ ), and Kirtland’s warbler  ( _Setophaga kirtlandii_ ) (U.S. Fish and

- 62 Wildlife Service 2012c).

- 63 Understanding that there may be some unintended fatalities of endangered species at

- 64 wind power facilities, the US Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) has begun issuing Incidental

- 65 Take Permits (ITPs), permitting certain levels of take at wind power facilities. In 2006, Kaheawa

- 66 Wind Project in Hawaii became the first wind power project in the US to receive a take permit

- 67 for species protected by the ESA (Hawaiian hoary bat, Hawaiian petrel, Hawaiian goose, and

- 68 Newell shearwater (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2007), and recently USFWS issued its first

- 69 ITP to a wind energy company to kill endangered species (Indiana bat and Virginia big-eared

- 70 bat) on the US mainland (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2013c). Incidental take permits for

- 71 Indiana bats are under consideration by USFWS at sites in Indiana (U.S. Fish and Wildlife

- 72 Service 2013a), Ohio (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2012a),  Maryland (U.S. Fish and Wildlife

- 73 Service 2012b), and Missouri (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2010, 2012c). In 2014, an ITP was

- 74 issued to allow a wind power company to kill up to five golden eagles over a five-year period

- 75 (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2014a), and USFWS is actively considering ITPs for golden

- 76 eagles at many other sites in the US (Clarke 2013).

- 77 Permitting take leads naturally to the question of estimating take. Take permits often

- 78 include mitigation requirements to compensate for estimated take. The level of mitigation is

- 79 determined by the best estimates of expected take calculated using collision-risk models, and

- 80 these models require field-based estimates of fatality to confirm the accuracy of their predictions.

- 81 Because overestimating potential take could result in costly and unjustified mitigation, whereas

- 82 underestimating could result in unanticipated declines in species populations already at risk,

- 83 collision-risk model estimates as well as field-based estimates need to be precise and accurate.

- 84 But confirming the accuracy of predicted take can be problematic. Often no carcasses are

- 85 observed, leading to the potentially misguided inference that no (or few) individuals have

- 86 actually been killed. This inference is justified only when the probability of observing an

- 87 individual is close to 1. As the probability of observing an individual decreases, the likelihood of

- 88 missing carcasses increases, making it unclear how to interpret having observed 0 carcasses.

- 89 A typical approach to estimating the number of birds or bats killed at a wind power

- 90 facility is for a field crew to search the ground beneath a subset of turbines at specified time

- 91 intervals and count the carcasses that show signs of having been killed by a turbine (U.S. Fish

- 92 and Wildlife Service 2012d). Carcass counts are adjusted for imperfect detection due to

- 93 scavengers, searcher error, and unsearched areas (Bispo et al. 2013; Huso 2011; Huso &

- 94 Dalthorp 2014; Korner-Nievergelt et al. 2011; Warren-Hicks et al. 2013). The most common

- 95 estimators of the total abundance of carcasses () at a site over an extended but fixed period of

- 96 time are variations or elaborations of /, where _X_ is the total number of carcasses observed

- 97 within a sampled area during the time period, and  is the estimated overall detection

- 98 probability, i.e., the probability of observing a carcass that was killed by any turbine at the site

- 99 during the time period of interest. Methods for determining  vary widely (Bernardino et al.

- 100 2013; Etterson 2014; MacKenzie et al. 2005; Warren-Hicks et al. 2013). A critical limitation of

- 101 these common approaches is that they necessarily yield [] 0 with no variance when 0

- 102 (e.g., Erickson et al. 2000; Huso 2011; Korner-Nievergelt et al. 2011; Peron et al. 2013;

- 103 Schoenfeld 2004; Warren-Hicks et al. 2013). A zero count can indicate that either no animals

- 104 were killed or that some (perhaps many) were killed but all the carcasses were missed in the

- 105 searches. With greater values of , we can more credibly make a case that  not a large number of

- 106 carcasses went undetected. But when ≪1, there is little assurance that the number killed was

- 107 0 even if no carcasses were observed 0. If the objective is to estimate take, observing no

- 108 carcasses when  is small offers little more than absence of evidence, rather than evidence of 109 absence.

- 110 Although we define our problem in terms of estimating take at a wind turbine facility, our

- 111 approach has application in many other situations where interest is in estimating a credible upper

- 112 bound of a superpopulation, where the population is open (individuals can leave the area), the

- 113 population may be small (perhaps even 0), and the probability of detection <1 (sometimes ≪1)

- 114 resulting in observed counts of 0. These include estimating the number of manatees that arrived

- 115 in and hence were exposed to an area contaminated by an oil spill (Martin et al. 2014), the

- 116 number of raptors killed by electrocution from transmission lines during a year (Lehman et al.

- 117 2007; Lehman et al. 2010), or the number of Indiana bats killed during a migratory season at a

- 118 wind power facility (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2012b).

- 119 There is a rich literature for estimating abundance of a superpopulation (Peron et al.

- 120 2013; Williams et al. 2011) or of an open population (Dail & Madsen 2011; Schwarz & Seber

- 121 1999; Seber 1982; White 2008), but the literature addressing estimating abundance when

- 122 observed count is 0, is  limited. Royle et al. (2005) have shown that concluding absence when

- 123 detection probability <1 and observed count is 0 introduces bias into the estimation of

- 124 abundance. Dupuis et al. (2011) propose a conditional approach to estimating occupancy rate of

- 125 a rare or hard to detect species, but it is conditioned on the true presence of the target species, a

- 126 condition that may not necessarily be met in our context. Recently, models that use simple

- 127 presence/absence have been developed to estimate abundance (MacKenzie et al. 2002, 2003;

- 128 Royle & Nichols 2003) but these models depend on actually observing at least some members of

- 129 the population. Fieberg et al. (2013) develop a Bayesian model-based approach to overcome the

- 130 inefficiencies of modified Horvitz-Thompson estimator when detection probabilities are low, but

- 131 their approach was not focused on estimation of abundance when no animals were observed.

- 132 Martin et al. (2014) derived estimates of both occupancy rate and upper bounds of the number of

- 133 manatees present at the time of sampling, even when no manatees were observed. However, their

- 134 approach restricts estimates to the time of sampling, and does not seek to estimate the total

- 135 number of individuals arriving over an extended period.

- 141 approach to estimating abundance rather than simple presence/absence when all samples are 0.

- 142 This analysis was motivated by discussions with the US Fish and Wildlife Service managers

- 351 **DISCUSSION**

- 352 Unless detection probability is 1, finding no carcasses does not provide assurance that no animals

- 353 have been killed. If even small numbers of fatalities are a concern, then Bayes' theorem can be

- 354 used to calculate a 100(1 % credible upper bound [] on the number of fatalities that have

- 355 occurred, even when no carcasses are observed during searches. The value of [] depends

- 356 strongly on both the detection probability  and on the uncertainty in the estimate of .

- 357 However, the influence of these factors is greatly diminished as  increases. When ~0.45

- 358 the difference in [] was never greater than a single animal.

- 359 Overall detection probability can often be increased by increasing the number of turbines

- 360 searched, increasing the area searched under each turbine, improving searcher efficiency (e.g., by

- 361 clearing vegetation, intensifying searches by narrowing search transect widths, using well-trained

- 362 dogs (Mathews et al. 2013), or searching more frequently. Searcher efficiency and carcass

- 363 persistence are key components of overall detection probability and are typically estimated by

- 364 means of placing and tracking trial carcasses throughout the sampling season. Increasing the

- 365 number of carcasses used in the trials increases the precision in estimates of , which in turn

- 366 decreases [] values.

- 367 Search data from previous years can be used to inform a subsequent year's prior to

- 368 improve the estimation of . This involves assumptions about how  varies from year to year.

- 369 Normally, the number of fatalities cannot be assumed to be the same each year, so assumptions

- 370 about how  varies through time must be made. With a constant population and a constant

- 371 probability of an individual being killed,  would be approximately distributed as a Poisson

- 372 random variable with variance equal to the mean. In practice, the fatality rate and the size of the

- 373 susceptible population would be expected to vary, so  would likely be more variable than a

- 374 Poisson. However, if  is assumed to follow a negative binomial distribution with large variance

- 375 ([] 5 or [] [] ) instead of a Poisson distribution ([] ) , the effect on  [] does not

- 376 appear to be large and the difference in [] from these assumed temporal distributions of  was

- 377 never greater than a single animal when  0.3.

- 378 Adjacent sites with similar landscape characteristics can have substantially differing

- 379 fatality rates (Arnett & Baerwald 2013; Arnett et al. 2008; deLucas et al. 2008; Drake et al.

- 380 2012), so using search data from one site or group of sites to inform the prior at a different site

- 381 may be difficult to justify.

- 382 Setting the credibility level 1  involves a compromise between maximizing

- 383 assurance that a specified level of take has not been exceeded when no carcasses are observed

- 384 and the implementation costs of achieving the detection probability to satisfy this level of

- 385 credibility. For example, for τ = 3,  | 00.2 can be achieved with 0.33,

- 386 whereas  | 00.01 requires 0.68 (Figure 5).

- 387 **Example Case**

- 388 Concerns about potential impacts of wind power development on populations of rare and

- 389 protected species have been growing since the late 1980s when reports of possibly hundreds of

- 390 raptors being killed by turbines in California were published (Orloff & Flannery 1992). Of

- 391 particular concern have been the large numbers of golden eagles ( _Aquila chrysaetos_ ) and smaller

- 392 numbers of bald eagles ( _Haliaeetus leucocephalus_ ) estimated to have been killed at sites across

- 393 the United States (Leslie et al. 2013; Pagel et al. 2013; Smallwood & Thelander 2008). A US

- 394 wind power company was recently convicted of violating the Migratory Bird Treaty Act

- 395 (MBTA) for killing 14 golden eagles and dozens of other birds at two wind power sites in

- 396 Wyoming (U.S. Department of Justice 2013). In 2009 the United States Fish and Wildlife

- 397 Service (USFWS) was granted the authority to issue incidental take permits (ITPs) for golden

- 398 eagles and bald eagles (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2009) that would allow power companies

- 399 to kill limited numbers of eagles as an unintended consequence of normal operations. Golden

- 400 eagle ITPs have been requested for at least 14 sites (Clarke 2013), but USFWS did not issue its

- 401 first ITP for eagles until June 2014, allowing the Shiloh IV Wind Project to kill up to five golden

- 402 eagles over a five-year period (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2014a). In 2013 USFWS changed

- 403 its permitting rules to allow issuance of 30-year take permits for eagles (U.S. Fish and Wildlife 404 Service 2013b).

- 405 We illustrate the application of our approach at a site in south-central Wyoming where

- 406 potential turbine-caused fatality of golden eagles was of concern (Young et al. 2003). Despite

- 407 high levels of use of the area by golden eagles, no carcasses were observed. However, five

- 408 carcasses of other raptor species were found during scheduled searches of the facility from

- 409 November 1998 through June 2002. The authors concluded that “due to low scavenger removal

- 410 rate and high searcher efficiency for medium and large carcasses it is likely that the [5 raptors]

- 411 found were the only raptors killed ... during the study period” suggesting that no golden eagles

- 412 were killed.

- 413 Using data presented in the report, we reconstruct  and calculate [] such that

- 414 [] | , 00.1. Because sampling protocol changed during the course of the

- 415 study, we restrict our evaluation to only the final year of monitoring, June 2001-June2002. The

- 416 facility is comprised of 69 0.6-MW turbines, approximately 40 meters at hub-height with rotor-

- 417 swept diameter of 42 meter and spaced approximately 84 meters apart. Every 28 days, trained

- 418 biologists searched for carcasses within 8-10 meter wide linear transects covering all areas

- 419 within 63 meters of a sample of half the turbines. Searchers removed each detected carcass after

- 420 recording the species, size, condition and location of discovery. Auxiliary to the search effort

- 421 from 1998-2001, researchers conducted experimental trials to estimate both searcher efficiency

- 422 and the distribution of carcass persistence times. At randomly selected times, carcasses of adult

- 423 female mallards (representing larger raptors) were placed within the study area and tested either

- 424 for their detection or persistence. No searcher efficiency or carcass persistence trials were

- 425 conducted June 2001-June 2002, so estimates from previous years were assumed to apply to this 426 period.

- 427 Given the information provided by Young, et al. (2003), we estimated , the overall

- 428 probability of detection for large carcasses, to be 0.335 (95% CI: 0.309, 0.355) (see Appendix II

- 429 for details) and assumed an uninformative uniform prior for . From this and the fact that no

- 430 golden eagles were found, we find that we can assert with only 34% credibility that no golden

- 431 eagles were killed, but we can assert with 90% credibility that no more than 5 golden eagles were

- 432 killed during this period. With this level of detection probability, the lack of evidence does not

- 433 support the suggestion that eagle take was indeed zero.

## 434 **Limitations**

- 435 An uninformative prior is likely the most reasonable option in the first year, but can result in

- 436 large differences in [] relative to an informative prior, particularly when  is low. However,

- 437 conflict over choice of an appropriate initial prior can be deflated by assuring   is at least 0.45

- 438 because the effect of the prior on [] is minimal when  is at this level.

- 439 We do not address methods for estimating . The factors affecting  include searcher

- 440 efficiency, carcass persistence times, search intervals, the proportion of carcasses expected to fall

- 441 in the searched area, the sampling fraction of the turbines, and spatial and temporal variation in

- 442 all these factors. The point of this exercise is not to address methods of estimating , but to

- 443 provide insight into the effects of detection probability on credible intervals of total take. Our

- 444 finding that ~0.45 can result in relatively precise estimates of [] , even when 0,

- 445 supports the idea that with careful design, precise estimates are attainable.

- 446 **Conservation Implications**

- 447 When considering take in the context of the Endangered Species Act we are often concerned

- 448 with assuring that loss of a species either arising from a consistent source (e.g., power lines, light

- 449 houses, wind power facilities) or following a single lethal event (e.g., oil spill, blasting project)

- 450 does not exceed some limit within a certain area and time period. The credibility with which we

- 451 can assert that the limit has not been exceeded is dependent on the probability of observing an

- 452 individual in the population during monitoring to detect take. Monitoring programs for which the

- 453 probability of detection of an individual is low cannot provide precise information with which to

- 454 evaluate the actual effect of the lethal source. Furthermore, if observing no carcasses is

- 455 interpreted as evidence of no effect, or if there are negative consequences to finding carcasses

- 456 (e.g., expensive mitigation or prosecution), then there is a perverse incentive to design and

457 implement the most ineffective search protocol possible, i.e., low overall detection probability.

458 If, on the other hand, there are negative consequences to large values of [] (e.g., expensive

- 459 mitigation) due to low probability of detection, then there will be strong incentive to design 460 monitoring protocol to achieve the highest overall detection probability possible.

- 461 When a monitoring protocol is designed to achieve a relatively high probability of 462 detection, results can also inform models of risk, providing feedback to refine models to improve 463 their predictive capacity. Increasing the probability of detection will increase credibility, and

- 464 high levels of credibility are needed when exceeding the set limit could result in further, perhaps 465 irreversible declines in a species at risk, or could result in expensive but perhaps unnecessary 466 mitigation efforts to offset the loss.

- 467 Without 100% probability of detection, it will be impossible to assert that no take has

- 468 occurred, even when no carcasses are observed. When probability of detection is high, observing 469 no carcasses can be construed as evidence that no or few animals have been killed, i.e., evidence

- 470 of absence. When probability of detection is low, however, finding zero carcasses does not

- 471 credibly rule out the possibility of a large take. We are left with only absence of evidence. While

- 472 many factors influence [] , our work indicates that their influence is minimal when ~0.45. 473 The actual target level of  will depend on the set take limit (τ), and the 1001 %

- 474 credible level, but not on species, in a general sense. Of course, achieving a given target level of 475  will be much more difficult for a small cryptic species at a site with dense vegetation or steep

- 476 terrain (e.g., a bat at a wind facility in the Adirondack Mountains) than for a large, easily

- 477 observed species in flat, open terrain with little vegetation (e.g., an eagle in the Mojave desert).

- 478 But given the same τ and α, the target level of  will be the same.

479 This analysis was motivated by discussions with the US Fish and Wildlife Service

- 480 managers concerned with assuring that a set level of take of Indiana bats was not exceeded at

- 481 wind power facilities, but our approach applies to any species for which detection probability can

- 482 be estimated and any situation in which the sampling fraction is known or estimable, e.g. oil

- 483 spills, power line or fence line searches, etc.
